\setcounter{chapter}{13}\mxunit{terminale-c12}{Random variables, concentration and the law of large numbers}\label{ch:14}

{\small\sffamily\color{mxmint}S62, S64, S73, S74, S77\par}

\begin{keypoint}[Objectives]Calculate the expected value and variance of a sum and of a mean; apply the Bienaymé--Chebyshev inequality; determine a sample size.\end{keypoint}

\section{Course notes}
\subsection{Sums and transformations}
For a finite random variable $X$, taking the values $x_i$ with probabilities $p_i$,
\[E(X)=\sum_i x_ip_i,\qquad V(X)=\sum_i(x_i-E(X))^2p_i=E(X^2)-E(X)^2.\]
The standard deviation is $\sigma(X)=\sqrt{V(X)}$. Expanding the square in $V(aX+b)$, the shift $b$ cancels and the factor $a$ is squared.
For finite random variables $X,Y$ and real numbers $a,b$,
\[E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y),\quad E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b,\quad V(aX+b)=a^2V(X).\]
The linearity of the expected value does not require independence. If $X,Y$ are independent, $V(X+Y)=V(X)+V(Y)$ (accepted without proof). Without this assumption, this formula cannot be applied. The standard deviation of $aX+b$ is $|a|\sigma(X)$.
\paragraph{Example of dependence.} If $Y=X$, then $V(X+Y)=V(2X)=4V(X)$, and not $2V(X)$ as soon as $V(X)\ne0$.
\paragraph{Proof for the binomial distribution.} Write $X=B_1+\cdots+B_n$ with the independent indicators of the successes. Each $B_i$ satisfies $E(B_i)=p$, $E(B_i^2)=p$ and $V(B_i)=p-p^2$. By linearity and additivity under independence, $E(X)=np$, $V(X)=np(1-p)$.
\subsection{Sample and mean}
A sample of size $n$ of a distribution is a family of $n$ independent random variables with the same distribution. If they have expected value $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, we write $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$ and $M_n=\frac{S_n}{n}$.
\begin{keypoint}[Sum and mean]
\[E(S_n)=n\mu,\quad V(S_n)=n\sigma^2,\qquad E(M_n)=\mu,\quad V(M_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\quad\sigma(M_n)=\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}.\]
\end{keypoint}
To divide the standard deviation of the mean by $2$, multiply the size by $4$. The variance of the sum increases; that of the mean decreases.
\subsection{Concentration}
\begin{keypoint}[Bienaymé--Chebyshev inequality]
For a random variable with expected value $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$, and $\delta>0$,
\[P(|X-\mu|\ge\delta)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\delta^2}.\]
An upper bound greater than $1$ remains true, but gives no further information; it can be replaced by $1$.
\end{keypoint}
\paragraph{Proof in the finite case.} In $V(X)=\sum_x(x-\mu)^2P(X=x)$, keep only the values satisfying $|x-\mu|\ge\delta$. Each square is then at least $\delta^2$. Hence $V(X)\ge\delta^2P(|X-\mu|\ge\delta)$.
\subsection{Law of large numbers}
Applied to the mean of a sample,
\[P(|M_n-\mu|\ge\delta)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{n\delta^2}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.\]
This is the law of large numbers in the setting considered: for a fixed precision, the probability of a deviation at least equal to this precision tends to zero. This result does not say that each realisation approaches $\mu$ monotonically.
\begin{method}[Choosing a sufficient size]
To guarantee $P(|M_n-\mu|<\delta)\ge1-\alpha$, it suffices to choose
\[n\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha\delta^2}.\]
Take the ceiling. This gives the smallest integer satisfying \emph{this bound}, not necessarily the minimum size for the exact probability.
\end{method}
For a frequency of successes, $\mu=p$ and $\sigma^2=p(1-p)\le\frac{1}{4}$. If $p$ is unknown, $n\ge\frac{1}{4\alpha\delta^2}$ is a uniform guarantee.


\section{Research activity}\textbf{Fluctuations of a frequency --- 40 min.}\par A fair coin is tossed independently. For every integer $n\ge1$, let $F_n$ be the frequency of ``heads'' among the first $n$ tosses.
\begin{enumerate}\item Write a program that simulates 1000 tosses, then plot the points $(n;F_n)$ for $1\le n\le1000$. Does the deviation from $\frac12$ necessarily decrease at every toss?
\item Express $E(F_n)$ and $V(F_n)$ in terms of $n$.
\item Using Bienaymé--Chebyshev, find an upper bound for $P(|F_{1000}-\frac12|\ge0.05)$.
\item Determine an integer $n$ sufficient for $P(|F_n-\frac12|<0.05)\ge0.99$.
\item State what the simulated trajectory shows and what the inequality obtained guarantees. Does a single simulation constitute a proof of this guarantee?\end{enumerate}

\section{Progressive exercises}

\mxexerciseitem{1}{Practice}Let $X$ be a random variable such that $E(X)=3$ and $V(X)=2$. Let $Y=4X-1$. Calculate the expected value, the variance and the standard deviation of $Y$.

\mxexerciseitem{2}{Practice}The random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent and satisfy $E(X)=2$, $E(Y)=5$, $V(X)=1$ and $V(Y)=4$. Calculate $E(2X-Y)$ and $V(2X-Y)$.

\mxexerciseitem{3}{Practice}Consider 64 independent random variables with the same distribution, with expected value $10$ and standard deviation $4$. Calculate the expected value and the standard deviation of their mean.

\mxexerciseitem{4}{Practice}Let $X$ be a random variable such that $E(X)=100$ and $V(X)=9$. Using the Bienaymé--Chebyshev inequality, give an upper bound for $P(|X-100|\ge6)$.

\mxexerciseitem{5}{Practice}Let $M_n$ be the mean of $n$ independent random variables with the same distribution, with expected value $\mu$ and variance $4$. Determine a size $n$ sufficient for $P(|M_n-\mu|<0.2)\ge0.95$.

\section{Homework}\textbf{Homework 14 --- Quality of an estimate --- 55 min.}\par We repeat $n\ge1$ independent Bernoulli trials with the same parameter $p\in[0;1]$, which is unknown. Let $F_n$ be the frequency of successes.
\begin{enumerate}\item Prove that $E(F_n)=p$ and $V(F_n)=\frac{p(1-p)}n$.
\item Show that $p(1-p)\le\frac14$ for all $p\in[0;1]$.
\item Deduce a size $n$ sufficient for $P(|F_n-p|<0.02)\ge0.95$, whatever the value of $p$.
\item We now know that $p\le0.1$. Determine a sharper upper bound for $p(1-p)$, then improve the sufficient size obtained in question 3.
\item For this question only, the $n$ results are all equal to the same Bernoulli variable $B$ with parameter $p$. Calculate $F_n$ and its variance. Explain why the previous guarantee no longer applies.\end{enumerate}

\ifmxteacher\mxnewpage\section{Teaching notes and solutions}\begin{teachernote}[Teacher notes]Test 5 and the second mock exam come before S73: do not ask for Bienaymé--Chebyshev or the law of large numbers in them. For the variance, have students circle the independence assumption. For concentration, distinguish the exact probability from the bound, and a sufficient rank from the true minimal rank. A simulation is not a proof, and an observed mean does not necessarily get closer with each new trial.\end{teachernote}

\subsection{Solutions to the activity}\begin{enumerate}
\item 
\begin{lstlisting}
from random import Random

def trajectoire_piece(N=1000, graine=2026):
    rng = Random(graine)
    piles, frequences = 0, []
    for n in range(1, N+1):
        piles += rng.random() < 0.5
        frequences.append(piles/n)
    return frequences
\end{lstlisting}
Plot the points $(n,F_n)$ with the list obtained. After two tosses giving one head and one tail, $F_2=\frac{1}{2}$. Whatever the third result, $F_3$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{2}{3}$: the deviation from $\frac{1}{2}$ increases. Stabilisation is not a monotonic decrease of the deviation along each trajectory.

\item Let $B_i$ be the indicator of heads. Then $F_n=\frac{B_1+\cdots+B_n}{n}$. Each $B_i$ has expected value $\frac{1}{2}$ and variance $\frac{1}{4}$. By linearity, $E(F_n)=\frac{1}{2}$; by independence and rescaling, $V(F_n)=\frac{n(\frac{1}{4})}{n^2}=\frac{1}{4n}$.
\item Bienaymé--Chebyshev gives $P(|F_{1000}-\frac{1}{2}|\ge0.05)\le\frac{1}{4\times1000\times0.05^2}=0.1$. This is an upper bound, not the exact probability.
\item To ensure a complementary probability of at most $0.01$, it suffices that $\frac{1}{4n\times0.05^2}\le0.01$. This is equivalent to $n\ge10000$. Then $P(|F_n-\frac{1}{2}|<0.05)\ge0.99$.
\item The simulation illustrates one finite realisation; other seeds give other trajectories. The inequality establishes a guarantee on the probability, for any sample satisfying the assumptions of independence and common distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{E1.}The affine transformation gives $E(4X-1)=4E(X)-1=11$ and $V(4X-1)=4^2V(X)=32$. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{32}=4\sqrt2$; the shift $-1$ does not change the dispersion.

\paragraph{E2.}By linearity, $E(2X-Y)=2E(X)-E(Y)=4-5=-1$. The independence of $X,Y$ allows us to add the variances of $2X$ and $-Y$: $V(2X-Y)=4V(X)+V(Y)=4+4=8$.

\paragraph{E3.}The mean of $64$ independent variables with the same distribution keeps the expected value $10$. Its variance is $\frac{4^2}{64}=\frac{1}{4}$, so its standard deviation is $\frac{1}{2}$.

\paragraph{E4.}Bienaymé--Chebyshev with $\delta=6$ gives $P(|X-100|\ge6)\le \frac{V(X)}{6^2}=\frac{9}{36}=\frac{1}{4}$. This bound gives neither an equality nor an exact value.

\paragraph{E5.}We have $P(|M_n-\mu|\ge0.2)\le\frac{4}{n\times0.2^2}=\frac{100}{n}$. For this bound to be at most $0.05$, it suffices that $n\ge2000$. The complement then has probability at least $0.95$.

\subsection{Solutions to Homework 14}\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $B_i$ be the independent indicators of the successes. $F_n=(\frac{1}{n})\sum_{i=1}^nB_i$, with $E(B_i)=p$, $V(B_i)=p(1-p)$. Hence
\[E(F_n)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n p=p,\qquad V(F_n)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^np(1-p)=\frac{p(1-p)}n.\]
\item $p(1-p)=p-p^2=\frac{1}{4}-(p-\frac{1}{2})^2\le\frac{1}{4}$. Equality is attained for $p=\frac{1}{2}$.
\item For all $p\in[0,1]$, $P(|F_n-p|\ge0.02)\le\frac{1}{4n\times0.02^2}$. It suffices that this bound be at most $0.05$, that is $n\ge12500$. By complement, this size guarantees the required probability, uniformly in $p$.
\item On $[0,0.1]$, the function $p\mapsto p(1-p)$ is increasing because its derivative $1-2p$ is positive. Hence $p(1-p)\le0.1\times0.9=0.09$. It now suffices that $n\ge\frac{0.09}{0.05\times0.02^2}=4500$. These sizes are sufficient in the sense of the bound, not necessarily minimal for the exact probability.
\item If all the trials copy the same variable $B$, then $F_n=\frac{B+\cdots+B}{n}=B$. Hence $V(F_n)=p(1-p)$, with no division by $n$. Adding the variances was allowed only because of independence; this assumption disappears here. For $0<p<1$, increasing the number of copies brings no new information.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Solutions to the textbook or past-paper work}$M_N$ is the mean number of universal donors per sample of $100$ people. Linearity gives $E(M_N)=7.14$; independence gives $V(M_N)=\frac{6.63}N$.
\[P(|M_N-7.14|\ge0.14)\le\frac{6.63}{0.14^2N}.\]
To make this bound at most $0.05$, it suffices to take
\[N\ge\left\lceil\frac{6.63}{0.05\times0.14^2}\right\rceil=6766.\]
By complement, $P(7<M_N<7.28)\ge0.95$.
